## References

1. [Mock Worlds, Real Skills: Building Small Agentic Language Models with Synthetic Tasks, Simulated Environments, and Rubric-Based Rewards](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.22511)
2. Code: [haruhi-sudo/SYNTHAGENT @ 00858b6](https://github.com/haruhi-sudo/SYNTHAGENT)

# Notes

## The problem: RL for small agents is starved of two things

The goal is to make an 8B or 14B model behave like a much bigger agent on multi-turn tool-use tasks: booking flights, fixing a telecom account, clarifying a missing parameter before calling an API. Reinforcement learning is the tool of choice here because it lets the model explore and learn from its own mistakes rather than copy a teacher. The authors (Lyu, Wang, Shen, Huang, Xu; USTC / Xi'an Jiaotong) argue that most agentic-RL papers tune the algorithm, while the real bottleneck sits upstream in two places.

The first bottleneck is data. Open agentic datasets are mostly math and web-search questions that need one tool (a code interpreter or a search engine). Modern base models have often seen them already, so when you sample 16 rollouts per prompt, nearly all of them succeed. If every rollout gets the same reward, a group-relative method like GRPO computes zero advantage for all of them and the prompt teaches nothing (this is exactly the failure that [[zero-gradient-prompt-filtering]] tries to patch after the fact; here the authors try to prevent it at generation time).

The second bottleneck is the environment. Training on real APIs needs millions of calls, real services rate-limit or change, they cover a narrow set of tools, and there is no user to talk to. A real API also cannot be reset cheaply between rollouts of the same task.

SynthAgent's answer is to fake the whole world with LLMs: invent the task, invent the tools, simulate the tools' outputs, simulate the user, and grade the result with a task-specific checklist. The bet is that skills learned in a mock world transfer to real benchmarks (TAU-2 and BFCL-V4). This is the same bet as [[2511.01824 - Simia Simulating Environments with Reasoning Models for Agent Training]] and the "generative simulator" idea in [[Patronus AI - Generative Simulators]]; what SynthAgent adds is an explicit mechanism for three things those approaches leave loose: forcing interaction, keeping simulated tools consistent across rollouts, and deriving rewards from executed trajectories.

## Stage 1: inventing tasks and tools from personas

Every task starts from a persona drawn from Persona Hub, a collection of about one billion web-derived character descriptions (see [[persona-driven-synthetic-data-generation]]). The persona supplies a context such as "senior site reliability engineer, knows Linux/SQL/Docker, event: fix a database bug". A strong teacher model (Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507, run locally) then does three things from that context:

1. Infers a high-level workflow, meaning the 5-7 macro steps a person like that would take (check logs, identify error, verify database state, roll back).
2. Designs a task-specific set of virtual tools, written as OpenAI function-calling schemas: a name, a description, typed input parameters, and typed outputs. The tools do not exist anywhere; they are only descriptions. On average each task gets 4.1 tools.
3. Writes one forbidden behavior, phrased as "Tool X must NOT be used to do Y", with a plausible real-world reason (budget, maintenance, invalid data). Violating it fails the task.

The point of giving every task its own tool suite is that the model cannot memorize a fixed API. Across 15,096 tasks it sees tens of thousands of different function schemas, which the authors argue teaches "how to use a tool described to me" rather than "how to call `search`". Samples whose tools cannot be parsed as valid function-calling JSON are thrown out.

The forbidden behavior is also doing real work. Most RL tasks reward reaching a goal; a constraint forces the policy to plan around a restriction, which is closer to what TAU-2's airline policy documents demand ("do not change a basic-economy fare").

## Stage 2: the information gap, and why it is a gradient argument

This is the paper's most interesting idea. If you hand the agent the workflow ("check logs, then verify DB state, then roll back"), the optimal action sequence $a^\star$ is written in the prompt. Every rollout does the same thing, gets the same reward, and training stalls. The authors formalize why.

Take the policy gradient at a single step $t$. The expected update direction is $\mathbb{E}_{a_t \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot|s_t)}[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)\, A(s_t,a_t)]$, where $\pi_\theta$ is the policy, $s_t$ the state (the conversation so far), $a_t$ the action (a message or tool call), and $A(s_t,a_t)$ the advantage: how much better this action did than the baseline. Because the advantage is defined relative to a baseline, its mean under the policy is zero, so its second moment equals its variance. Cauchy-Schwarz then gives the bound (their Eq. 2):

$$\big\|\mathbb{E}[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)\,A(s_t,a_t)]\big\| \le \sqrt{\mathbb{E}\|\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)\|^2}\cdot\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_{a_t}[A(s_t,a_t)]}$$

In words: the gradient can be no larger than (how sensitive the log-probability is to the weights) times (how much the outcomes of different actions actually differ). If the prompt pins down the right action, every sampled action performs about the same, $\mathrm{Var}[A]\approx 0$ (Eq. 1), and the right-hand side collapses. The learning signal dies regardless of the algorithm.

The fix is to deliberately split the task's initial state $s_0$ into two pieces (Eq. 3):

$$s_0 \mapsto (I, C) \quad \text{s.t.}\quad H(a^\star \mid I) \gg \epsilon$$

$I$ is the instruction the agent sees; $C$ is a hidden context that only the simulated user knows. $H(a^\star|I)$ is the conditional entropy of the optimal action given only the instruction, i.e. how uncertain the right move is from what the agent can see. The constraint says: make $I$ vague enough that the right action is genuinely unclear. In practice an LLM rewrites the detailed request into one fuzzy sentence ("The checkout service is throwing 500 errors again. Can you verify and fix it?") and moves the decisive facts ("v2.1 was just deployed", "the API is out of memory") into $C$.

Now the agent must ask. Each answer $o_t$ lowers uncertainty, $H(a^\star|I, o_{\le t}) < H(a^\star|I)$, and the early choices matter: which question to ask first, whether to act before asking. Different rollouts make different early choices and get different outcomes, so advantage variance stays high and gradients stay alive.

A caveat worth stating. The inequality is an upper bound, and the practical algorithm is GRPO, which divides each rollout's advantage by the standard deviation of the group's rewards. That normalization rescales small-but-nonzero variance back up (see [[std-normalization-difficulty-bias-in-group-rl]]). So in GRPO the real killer is not "small variance" but "zero variance", i.e. all 16 rollouts earning identical reward. The information gap attacks that same failure; the derivation just motivates it with a cleaner, looser argument.

## Stage 3: simulating tools and users without breaking RL

When the agent calls one of the invented tools, a smaller model (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct) reads the tool description and the call, and writes a plausible response. When the agent asks the user a question, the same kind of model answers from the hidden context $C$, revealing it a little at a time. The authors used the small model because these jobs are "formatted question answering", and they test that claim later.

The subtle problem is consistency. RL samples the same task many times (16 rollouts per prompt here). If `read_logs("checkout-service")` returns "OutOfMemoryError" in one rollout and "disk full" in another, then identical state-action pairs lead to different futures, advantage estimates for the same action disagree in magnitude and even sign, and the gradient becomes noise. This is the RL version of the reproducibility problem in [[stochastic-llm-output-and-robustness-in-agent-simulations]].

The fix is a task-level finite mapping (Eq. 4):

$$M = \{(u_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{|M|}, \quad u_i = (\text{tool}_i, \text{args}_i)$$

Each entry records a call $u_i$ (tool name plus arguments) and the response $y_i$ that was given. On a new call, the simulator is shown the whole mapping, decides whether an equivalent call already exists, and either reuses its response or writes a new one and appends it. Because each task has its own tiny tool suite, the mapping stays small: the paper bounds it by 16 rollouts x 10 calls = 160 entries, and reports an average size of 30.1 after training. That is small enough to put straight into the simulator's prompt, so no retrieval system is needed, and the equivalence check and response generation happen in one forward pass. Semantic matching also means `read_logs("checkout")` and `read_logs("checkout-service")` can hit the same entry, which exact-match caching would miss.

## Stage 4: rubrics derived from execution, not from imagination

Math tasks have a checkable answer. Multi-step tool tasks do not, and a raw LLM judge assigning a 1-10 score is noisy and subjective. SynthAgent builds a per-task checklist instead, following the logic of [[instance-specific-rubric-as-reward-function]] and [[2507.17746 - Rubrics as Rewards (RaR)]].

The workflow from Stage 1 is an obvious source of subgoals, but a planned workflow may not match what actually happens when someone attempts the task. So the teacher solves each task several times in the mock environment (the paper uses four demonstrations), and a judge compares the trajectories against the workflow. If the workflow leaves too many steps unexecuted, the task is judged badly designed and discarded. This doubles as a data filter. Surviving tasks get a rubric with three sections:

1. Forbidden behaviors, inherited from Stage 1 (e.g., "must not transcribe audio longer than 90 seconds").
2. Subgoals, extracted from what the teacher actually did, stated at a level that allows several valid paths.
3. Required user interactions: facts the agent must ask for rather than assume.

The reward (Eq. 5) is

$$R(\tau) = \mathbb{I}(\tau)\cdot\big(N_{\text{subgoals}}(\tau) + I_{\text{user\_query}}(\tau)\big)$$

where $\tau$ is a trajectory, $\mathbb{I}(\tau)\in\{0,1\}$ is zero if any forbidden behavior occurred, $N_{\text{subgoals}}\in[0,1]$ is the fraction of subgoals completed, and $I_{\text{user\_query}}\in[0,1]$ is the fraction of required interactions satisfied. The text says the two fractions are averaged. The forbidden behavior acts as a multiplicative gate: break the rule and nothing else counts. During training Qwen3-30B-A3B judges each trajectory against its rubric.

The whole synthesis pipeline costs about 25,278 tokens per task on locally hosted open models.

## Stage 5: the training mix

Following the Kimi K2 and LongCat reports, which stress that agents need strong reasoning, the authors add 4,000 math and search problems sampled from ToolStar. Because these abstract problems look nothing like the persona-rich tool tasks, they rewrite each into a persona-based scenario with Qwen3-235B, solve each three times, and keep only problems where all three answers agree. Reasoning tasks run in a real Python sandbox and real Google search with correctness rewards; tool tasks run in the mock world with rubric rewards. Everything is trained together with GRPO in the VERL framework, in non-thinking mode, with no SFT warm-up (Qwen3 already follows the tool-call format). Paper hyperparameters: global batch 128, PPO mini-batch 16, 16 rollouts, 13,000-token max response, clip ratio 0.2 to 0.28 (the asymmetric "clip-higher" trick from [[2503.14476 - DAPO Open-Source LLM RL System at Scale]]), up to 16 turns, 2 epochs on 8 H20 GPUs.

## Experiments

Evaluation is on real environments, not the mock world. TAU-2 (airline 50 tasks, telecom 114, retail 114; Avg@4) runs the agent against a user simulated by Kimi-K2-Instruct, where users can also call tools and change state (see [[dual-control-environments]] and [[sierra-research-tau2-bench - Agent Evaluation Harness]]). BFCL-V4 multi-turn (4 subsets x 200) tests multi-turn function calling, missing functions, missing parameters, and long context. Success is exact match of the final environment state. Out-of-domain reasoning uses AIME24/25, HMMT25, OlympiadBench, FRAMES, xBench and WebWalker. All baselines are re-run on the December 2025 versions of the benchmarks with identical prompts and function-calling format.

Agentic results (Table 2, averaged over TAU-2 and BFCL subsets):

| Model | Airline | Telecom | Retail | BFCL Base | Miss Func | Miss Param | Long Ctx | Avg |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-235B | 47.5 | 37.7 | 68.0 | 58.5 | 47.5 | 35.0 | 54.0 | 49.7 |
| Qwen3-14B | 22.0 | 25.4 | 39.5 | 40.0 | 34.5 | 26.5 | 26.5 | 30.6 |
| Qwen3-32B | 22.5 | 27.6 | 44.7 | 50.5 | 43.0 | 30.5 | 33.0 | 36.0 |
| ToolStar-8B | 13.5 | 25.9 | 39.5 | 52.0 | 38.0 | 22.5 | 30.5 | 31.7 |
| ToolStar-14B | 18.0 | 30.7 | 40.4 | 56.5 | 35.5 | 29.5 | 39.5 | 35.7 |
| SynthAgent-8B | 34.5 | 38.2 | 57.2 | 54.5 | 45.5 | 33.0 | 37.5 | 42.9 |
| SynthAgent-14B | 40.0 | 44.7 | 58.6 | 57.0 | 46.5 | 31.0 | 46.0 | 46.3 |

The headline: an 8B model trained this way beats Qwen3-32B by 6.9 average points, and the 14B lands 3.4 points under Qwen3-235B. The biggest jumps are on TAU-2, the benchmark that most resembles the training setup (an under-informed agent talking to a user). "Matches Qwen3-235B on many domains" is generous: the 14B still trails by 7.5 on airline and 9.4 on retail, and actually beats it on telecom.

Two things in the table deserve a closer look. First, ToolStar training (30,000 math and search examples) is described as giving "no significant improvement" on agentic tasks, but ToolStar-14B scores 56.5 on BFCL Base versus 40.0 for plain Qwen3-14B. Reasoning-only data clearly helps BFCL; it just does not help TAU-2. Second, SynthAgent-14B is worse than SynthAgent-8B on Miss Func (31.0 vs 33.0), so scale does not help uniformly.

Reasoning transfer (Table 3): SynthAgent-8B averages 58.5 against 53.6 for ToolStar-8B, which was trained on 30,000 reasoning examples, despite SynthAgent seeing only 4,000. The 14B reaches 61.3.

The ablation (Table 4, Qwen3-8B) is where the design gets tested:

| Setting | Airline | Telecom | Retail | BFCL multi-turn |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-8B | 15.0 | 8.8 | 32.5 | 28.1 |
| Reasoning data only | 22.0 | 26.1 | 38.2 | 37.9 |
| No information gap | 22.0 | 28.9 | 35.3 | 39.1 |
| SynthAgent-8B | 34.5 | 38.2 | 57.2 | 42.6 |

Removing the information gap (giving the agent the explicit workflow and no user to talk to) makes the synthetic tool data almost worthless on TAU-2: retail drops from 57.2 to 35.3, below the reasoning-only run. That supports the gradient argument. The BFCL column tells a different story that the paper does not discuss: reasoning data alone moves BFCL from 28.1 to 37.9, and the full method adds only 4.7 more. Most of the BFCL gain is available without any mock world.

Further analyses, all on 5,000-task subsets with Qwen3-8B:

- Simulator size (Figure 3): training with a 235B tool simulator versus the 30B one gives 26.0 vs 25.5 airline, 35.5 vs 35.5 telecom, 52.2 vs 52.0 retail. The simulator does not need to be large. This matches the intuition in [[simulation-fidelity-limited-to-describable-environments]]: when the tool is fully described by its schema, simulating it is a formatting job.
- Teacher demonstrations for rubric building (Figure 4): 2, 3, or 4 demonstrations give nearly identical results (e.g., retail 51.5, 52.6, 52.2), because the rubric comes mostly from the workflow and the demonstrations only check it.
- Data scale and RL versus SFT (Figure 5): going from 5K to 15K tasks lifts TAU-2 (airline 26.0 to 34.5, telecom 35.5 to 38.2, retail 52.2 to 57.2). SFT on 15K Qwen3-235B trajectories gives 28.0, 32.2 and 43.0, well below RL on the same tasks. This echoes [[simulated-trajectories-match-real-at-equal-size]] from the Simia line of work, but pushes further: on the same synthetic data, exploration beats imitation.
- Judge stability (Figure 6): the variance of rubric scores falls from 1.8 at step 0 to 0.9 at step 96, then rises to 1.1 at step 192. The text calls this "increasingly consistent", which ignores the uptick, and it is ambiguous whether the variance is across repeated judgments of one trajectory (judge noise) or across freshly sampled trajectories (policy noise). As the policy converges, its own outputs become more uniform, which would lower variance even with an equally noisy judge.

## How the code implements it

The repo has two halves: `tool_use_data_synthesis/` (LangGraph pipelines calling Qwen3-235B for tool sets, fuzzy tasks, teacher solves, and rubrics) and `RL/` (a modified copy of VERL with a custom agent loop, parser, mock-tool class, and reward function). A 4,776-task training parquet is released, which is a subset of the 15,096 in the paper. The code shows several places where the implementation is cruder, or simply different, from the paper's description, and those gaps are the most useful part of reading it.

### 1. Making the task fuzzy and hiding the details

Problem: turn an over-specified workflow into a vague one-line request plus a private background that only the simulated user sees. This is the information gap $s_0 \mapsto (I, C)$.

`tool_use_data_synthesis/functions/fuzzy_task.py:17-32 @ 00858b6`
```python
2. Then, provide the task description, wrapped in <task></task> tags, it should not be too detailed, more information is presented in the next step:
<task>
(One‑sentence fuzzy task, it should be concise, and more information is provided in the next step)
</task>

3. Finally,provide additional task-related background information, including what must be understood to complete the task and key subtasks. Wrap this in tags:
<background>
(Background information Agent should know, it should be detailed)
</background>

The task and background description must:
- Not lengthy or too detailed.
- Avoid explicitly or implicitly instructing which tools to use. It's very important!
- Not directly provide the specific execution workflow.
- Have a clear and specific intent, allowing the intelligent agent to infer how to implement it.
- Include enough rich details so that the intelligent agent can naturally infer the need for multi-step, multi-tool integration.
```

The `<task>` becomes $I$ and the `<background>` becomes $C$. There is no entropy measurement anywhere; "$H(a^\star|I) \gg \epsilon$" is enforced purely by prompt instructions ("one-sentence", "not directly provide the specific execution workflow"). Note also that the RL training prompt (built in `virtual_tool_use_convert_parquet.py` and visible in the released parquet) tells the agent "The user most likely provided insufficient information... Please interact with the user multiple turns, the more times you interact, the more information you can gather." So the questioning behavior is also prompted directly, not only learned from the gap. The paper's ablation does not separate the effect of this instruction from the effect of the hidden context.

### 2. How "asking the user" becomes an action

Problem: the agent needs some way to talk to the user inside an RL rollout loop that only understands tool calls.

`RL/verl/experimental/agent_loop/tool_parser.py:120-131 @ 00858b6`
```python
    @rollout_trace_op
    async def extract_tool_calls(self, responses_ids: list[int]) -> tuple[str, list[FunctionCall]]:
        loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
        text = await loop.run_in_executor(None, self.tokenizer.decode, responses_ids)
        if self.tool_call_start_token not in text or self.tool_call_end_token not in text:
            if self.final_answer_token in text:
                return text, []

            # agent's query to the user
            function_calls = [FunctionCall(name="mock_user", arguments=json.dumps({"agent_query":text}, ensure_ascii=False))]
            
            return text, function_calls
```

This is the design choice the paper does not spell out. There is no "ask_user" tool. Any assistant turn that contains neither a `<tool_call>` nor an `<answer>` tag is treated as a question to the user and routed to a fake tool named `mock_user`. So each turn has exactly three outcomes: call a tool, finish, or talk. The benefit is that the agent asks questions in natural language, the way it would on TAU-2. The cost is that a malformed tool call (missing the closing tag) is silently sent to the user simulator as a question rather than flagged as an error.

### 3. Routing invented tools to the simulator

Problem: the tools in each task do not exist, so every call to one must be sent to the LLM simulator, while calls to real tools (the Python sandbox) must go to the real thing.

`RL/verl/experimental/agent_loop/tool_agent_loop.py:689-712 @ 00858b6`
```python
            # TODO: append malformed tool_call to the prompt: invalid function name or arguments
            tool_name = tool_call.name

            if tool_name in self.tools:
                tool_args = json.loads(tool_call.arguments)
                tool = self.tools[tool_name]
            else:
                tool_descriptions = re.findall(r"<tools>(.*?)</tools>", history_messages, re.DOTALL)[-1]
                # if tool_name == "none" or tool_name is None:
                #     breakpoint()
                if tool_name not in tool_descriptions and tool_name != "mock_user":
                    # logger.warning(f"Error when executing tool: tool {tool_name} not found")
                    return (
                        ToolResponse(
                            text=f"Error when executing tool: tool {tool_name} not found",
                        ),
                        0.0,
                        {},
                    )
                
                tool = self.tools["mock_tool"]
                mock_tool_args = {"name": tool_name, "arguments": json.loads(tool_call.arguments)}
                tool_name = "mock_tool"
                tool_args = {"mock_tool_name_and_args": json.dumps(mock_tool_args), "history_messages": history_messages}
```

Registered real tools are dispatched normally. For everything else, the loop re-reads the task's tool schemas from the decoded prompt and checks whether the name appears. Two details matter. The check `tool_name not in tool_descriptions` is a substring test on the raw schema text, so a hallucinated name that happens to appear anywhere in the descriptions (for example, a word inside another tool's description) passes and gets a simulated response instead of an error. And the whole decoded conversation (`history_messages`) is passed along, which the user simulator uses as dialogue history. Nothing here validates arguments against the schema; that job is left to the simulator's judgment.

### 4. The consistency mapping, as actually built

Problem: the same tool call across the 16 rollouts of a task must return the same answer, or advantage estimates become noise.

`RL/my_script/tools/mock_tool.py:337-359 @ 00858b6`
```python
            # Extract tool response
            tool_response_matches = re.findall(r"<response>(.+?)</response>", all_content, re.DOTALL)
            if tool_response_matches:
                last_match = tool_response_matches[-1]
                tool_response = last_match.strip()
            else:
                tool_response = None
            
            # Extract is_new flag
            is_new_matches = re.findall(r"<is_new>(.+?)</is_new>", all_content, re.DOTALL)
            is_new = False
            if is_new_matches:
                is_new_str = is_new_matches[-1].strip().lower()
                is_new = is_new_str == "true"

            if is_new:
                if len(world_state) < 100:
                    world_state.append(f"Query:\n{mock_tool_name_and_args}\nResponse:\n{tool_response}")
                    with file_lock:
                        with open(save_tool_call_path, "w") as f:
                            json.dump(world_state, f, indent=4, ensure_ascii=False)
            
            return tool_response
```

The mapping $M$ is a JSON list of "Query/Response" strings in a file at `<root>/<task_id>/tool_call_history.json`. The simulator LLM itself decides equivalence and reports it in an `<is_new>` tag; only calls it labels as new are appended. Several things differ from the paper's picture:

- The mapping is capped at 100 entries, not 160.
- The file is read under a lock earlier (lines 275-277), then the LLM is called with no lock held, then the whole list is written back. With 16 rollouts of one task running concurrently, two rollouts can both read the same old list, both add a new entry, and the second write erases the first. Entries can be silently lost, which weakens exactly the consistency the mapping is meant to guarantee.
- The mapping is a file that persists, so it survives across epochs and across training runs unless the directory is cleared. It is "task-level", but not "rollout-group-level" as the paper's 16 x 10 bound suggests.
- The simulator prompt tells the model that if several stored calls match, it should "randomly select one to reuse". That is a small source of inconsistency built in on purpose.
- The teacher-solving stage writes to the same file layout (`output/solve_tool_use/<id>/tool_call_history.json`). The RL converter defaults to a different directory (`tmp/solve_tool_use`), but pointing it at the synthesis output would pre-seed the RL mapping with the teacher's tool responses. The paper does not say which was done.

The simulator also runs at temperature 0.9 by default, so when a call is new, its response is sampled with high randomness.

### 5. The reward function, as actually built

Problem: turn a free-text rubric into a scalar reward via an LLM judge.

`RL/my_script/reward_function.py:293-313 @ 00858b6`
```python
        score = 0
        total_sec_count = 0
        for section in result['section_scores']:
            if section["name"].strip().startswith("Policy"):
                if section['total'] == 0 or section['score'] / section['total'] < 0.5:
                    return 0.0
                continue

            if section['total'] != 0:
                if section["name"].strip().startswith("Task"):
                    if section['score'] / section['total'] < 0.3:
                        return 0.0
                    score += (0.7 * section['score'] / section['total'])
                else:
                    score += (0.3 * section['score'] / section['total'])
    
                total_sec_count += 1
        # breakpoint()
        if total_sec_count == 0:
            print("total_sec_count is 0")
        return score if total_sec_count > 0 else 0.3
```

The judge (prompted as "a very strict evaluator who only approves of perfect answers") writes a "Completed Items: X/Y" line for each of three sections, and this code turns those counts into a score. It differs from Eq. 5 in four ways:

- **The forbidden-behavior gate is a threshold, not "any violation".** The episode is zeroed only if fewer than half the policy criteria pass. The rubric generator asks the judge to "list as many reasonable policies as possible", and the released rubrics usually have two policy items: the inherited forbidden behavior (1a) and "don't invent parameters without asking" (1b). With two items, violating the forbidden behavior while passing 1b gives 1/2 = 0.5, which is not below 0.5, so the episode keeps its reward. The paper's claim that any forbidden behavior yields zero reward does not hold in this code whenever there are two or more policy criteria.
- **Weights are 0.7 for subgoals and 0.3 for user interaction**, not the equal average the text describes.
- **There is a hidden floor.** If fewer than 30% of subgoals are completed, reward is zero. That turns the low end of the reward into a step function, which makes it sparser than Eq. 5 implies.
- **Parse failures earn 0.3.** If the judge output has no parseable sections (including when all API retries fail and `call_llm_api` returns the string "No message"), `total_sec_count` stays 0 and the function returns 0.3 rather than 0. A trajectory the judge could not evaluate is paid about the same as one that completes roughly 40% of its subgoals. This is a straightforward reward-noise channel of the type catalogued in [[2605.12474 - Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning]] and [[verifier-failure-vs-rubric-design-failure]].

The judge also sees the whole decoded solution, including simulated tool outputs, so it grades against whatever world the simulator invented in that rollout.

### 6. The data filter

Problem: throw away tasks whose planned workflow does not match what execution actually looks like.

`tool_use_data_synthesis/rubrics.py:320-328 @ 00858b6`
```python
    # Extract alignment_check
    alignment_check_match = re.search(r'<alignment_check>(.*?)</alignment_check>', response_content, re.DOTALL)
    if alignment_check_match:
        result["alignment_check"] = alignment_check_match.group(1).strip()
    else:
        logger.warning("Alignment check section not found in response")

    if result["alignment_check"] == "" or "discard" in result["alignment_check"].lower():
        return result
```

The "workflow alignment check" in the paper is this: if the word "discard" appears anywhere in the judge's alignment section, the task is dropped. The prompt asks for "KEEP/DISCARD decisions" per solution, so a judge that writes "no reason to DISCARD" or discards one of several solutions also kills the whole task. That makes the filter stricter than intended rather than laxer, which is the safer direction, but it means the retention rate reflects wording as much as quality. Also note the configs: `solve_task.yaml` sets `repeat_times: 2` teacher solves per run and `rubrics.yaml` reads the top 3 solution files, while the paper says four demonstrations were used. Figure 4 suggests this does not matter much.

### Other config differences

`run_virtual_tool.sh` uses batch 64, max response 8,192, 10 turns, 1 epoch, KL coefficient 0, and the DAPO reward manager. The paper reports batch 128, 13,000 tokens, 16 turns, 2 epochs. The README also recommends training on reasoning tasks first and then on virtual tool tasks, i.e. two sequential stages, while the paper describes one combined dataset.

## What is interesting, and what to be careful about

The strongest idea is the one in the ablation: the value of synthetic agentic data comes less from the tools than from withholding information. A mock world with full instructions was nearly useless on TAU-2; the same world with hidden context and a user to question produced most of the gain. That fits a general principle behind [[agentic-tasks-are-artifact-bundles-not-dataset-rows]]: a task is not a question, it is a question plus the environment that makes it uncertain.

The second is that simulator quality is not the bottleneck. A 30B simulator worked as well as a 235B one. If that holds up, mock environments are cheap enough to scale much further, which changes the cost trade-off discussed in [[environment-task-split-sets-the-cost-model]].

Genuine limitations:

- **Single runs, small test sets, no error bars.** TAU-2 airline has 50 tasks, so one task is 2 points; several key comparisons (e.g. simulator size, 26.0 vs 25.5) are well inside noise.
- **Evaluation leans toward the training format.** TAU-2 is an under-informed agent talking to a simulated user, which is exactly what training rehearses. The gains there are largest; on BFCL much of the gain comes from reasoning data alone.
- **The judge is a 30B model grading its own kind of world.** Everything inside a training episode (tool outputs, user replies, grade) comes from Qwen3 models. No human audit of simulator fidelity, user leakage, or judge accuracy is reported. The user-simulator auditing concerns in [[llm-user-simulator-design-and-auditing]] and the judge ceiling in [[judge-reasoning-ceiling-bounds-gradable-skills]] apply directly.
- **Reward-hacking surface.** Because the judge reads simulated tool outputs and interaction counts, a policy could be rewarded for asking many questions (the prompt even encourages it) and for trajectories whose simulated outputs look successful. The paper does not report question counts beyond an average of 13.4 interactions per task after training, or check for over-asking.
- **The code and paper disagree on the reward**, as shown above, so reproducing the paper's numbers from Eq. 5 alone would train a different objective.
- **Baseline scope.** The only trained baseline is ToolStar, a math/search dataset, so the comparison shows "diverse synthetic tool data beats narrow reasoning data" more than it shows SynthAgent beats other agentic synthesis pipelines (APIGen-MT, Simia, etc.). The authors acknowledge that leading labs do not release their synthetic data, which limits comparison.

## Key claims

1. **Synthetic tasks in a mock world make an 8B model beat Qwen3-32B on real agentic benchmarks.** SynthAgent-8B averages 42.9 against 36.0 for Qwen3-32B and 30.6 for Qwen3-14B. Setup: Qwen3-8B trained with GRPO (non-thinking) on 15,096 synthetic tool tasks plus 4,000 reasoning tasks, evaluated on TAU-2 (Avg@4, Kimi-K2 user) and BFCL-V4 multi-turn, December 2025 versions.
   > On TAU-2 and BFCL-Multi-turn, S YNTH AGENT-8B scores 42.9 on average (+12.3 over Qwen3-14B, and +6.9 over Qwen3-32B).
   (Section 4.2, Table 2)

2. **The 14B version gets within 3.4 points of Qwen3-235B.** 46.3 vs 49.7 average; the gap is larger on airline and retail. Same setup with Qwen3-14B.
   > The improvements are even greater with S YNTH AGENT-14B, which scores 46.3 on average.
   (Section 4.2, Table 2)

3. **Without the information gap, synthetic tool data gives almost no benefit.** TAU-2 retail falls from 57.2 to 35.3 and airline from 34.5 to 22.0 when workflows are given explicitly and no user interaction is used. Setup: Qwen3-8B ablation.
   > However, if we do not introduce information gaps, do not rewrite workflows into less explicit descriptions, and directly use them for training without user interaction, the benefit of tool-use data becomes negligible.
   (Section 4.3, Table 4)

4. **Hiding facts in a user-only context is what forces interaction.** No number on its own; supported by claim 3.
   > This design forces agents to actively query users and call tools to recover missing information, encouraging genuine long-horizon interaction.
   (Section 1)

5. **A 30B tool simulator is as good as a 235B one for training.** TAU-2 airline 26.0 vs 25.5, telecom 35.5 vs 35.5, retail 52.2 vs 52.0. Setup: Qwen3-8B, 5,000 synthetic tasks, single runs.
   > Both are simple, well-defined operations that typically do not require a strong model.
   (Section 4.3, Figure 3)

6. **Per-task consistency needs only a small in-prompt mapping, not retrieval.** Average mapping size 30.1 after training, bounded at 160 in the paper's analysis (the code caps at 100).
   > Empirically, the task-level mapping remains very small.
   (Section 3.2, Table 1)

7. **Two teacher demonstrations are enough to build rubrics.** Retail 51.5 / 52.6 / 52.2 for 2 / 3 / 4 demonstrations. Setup: Qwen3-8B, 5,000 tasks.
   > As shown in Figure 4, adding more demonstrations yields no significant gains, suggesting rubric construction does not require substantial computation.
   (Section 4.3, Figure 4)

8. **RL beats SFT on the same synthetic tasks, and more data keeps helping.** 15K RL: 34.5 / 38.2 / 57.2 on airline / telecom / retail; 15K SFT on Qwen3-235B trajectories: 28.0 / 32.2 / 43.0; 5K RL: 26.0 / 35.5 / 52.2. Setup: Qwen3-8B on TAU-2.
   > SFT yields much smaller gains than RL, as RL can generate far more diverse trajectories through exploration, which is a crucial factor for improving agentic behavior.
   (Appendix B, Figure 5)

9. **Tool-use training transfers to math and search reasoning.** SynthAgent-8B averages 58.5 on seven reasoning benchmarks against 53.6 for ToolStar-8B, trained on 30,000 reasoning examples. Setup: non-thinking mode, real Python and Google Search tools.
   > Under the same non-thinking setting, S YNTH AGENT-8B significantly outperforms Qwen3-14B and even exceeds an 8B model trained on 30,000 ToolStar examples.
   (Section 4.2, Table 3)

10. **The synthesis pipeline is cheap.** About 25,278 tokens per task, all on locally hosted open models.
    > Since the entire process runs on locally deployed open-source models, the cost is negligible.
    (Section 3.3, Table 1)

11. **In the released code, a forbidden-behavior violation does not always zero the reward.** The gate triggers only when fewer than half of policy criteria pass, and released rubrics commonly have two policy criteria. This contradicts the paper's Eq. 5 description. Setup: `compute_score_virtual_tool` in the released repo.
    > if section['total'] == 0 or section['score'] / section['total'] < 0.5:
    (`RL/my_script/reward_function.py:297 @ 00858b6`)
